cues.text: Two Men in the Communion Line
On the Monday after Easter in 1604, Father Salvatore Spiga was distributing Communion.
He was pastor of St. Bernard’s church in Mogoro, on the Italian island of Sardinia, when two men well known for their dissolute lives came forward to receive it.
Spit Out at the Altar Rail
The priest gave them Communion as he would any other communicant, but the instant the Hosts touched their tongues, both men spit them out onto the stone floor beneath the altar rail.

When questioned, they explained that the Host had felt burning hot, like a live ember, scorching their mouths — and, struck with sudden remorse at having approached Communion without first going to confession, both fled the church.
A Mark That Would Not Wash Away
When Father Salvatore went to retrieve the fallen Hosts, he found they had left a visible imprint burned into the stone floor itself.
Repeated attempts to clean the marks away proved futile; the imprints remained fixed in the stone regardless of how thoroughly the area was scrubbed.
The event is confirmed in a notarized public act drawn up by the notary Pedro Antonio Escano on May 25, 1686.
It records a contract for a wooden tabernacle built over the main altar, with an opening specifically left so the marked 'Stone of the Miracle' remained visible to the faithful behind glass.
The stone, bearing the imprints, is preserved there to this day.

Mogoro still marks the event every year with a solemn Eucharistic procession on the Sunday after Easter, held in reparation for the original sacrilege as much as in celebration of the sign that followed it.
The Mogoro account belongs to a distinct, smaller category of Eucharistic tradition.
It centers not on preservation or transformation but on visible consequence—an imprint left in stone and deliberately kept in view.
This serves as a permanent physical reminder of a single Communion given without proper preparation.
